## A Crumbling Facade

Earlier this year, I had decided I wanted to take my career to the next level.

I wanted to work on bigger and more challenging projects, so I interviewed with several FAANG and FAANG-adjacent companies.

I went through the typical Reddit interview prep stack. I Leetcoded, online-coursed, and Youtubed my way to final round after final round of each interview process. The recruiters told me how great each preceding round went and that feedback was "so far, so good", which left me in surreal disbelief that I'd made it so far through these notoriously difficult interviews and a beaming hope that my dreams would soon come true... until the emails with the final decisions arrived a week later.

They all read along the same lines.

> "Thank you for your interest in exploring career opportunities with <INSERT_COMPANY> and taking time to interview for the <INSERT_POSITION> opportunity. We were impressed with your skills and experience, however, the team has decided not to move forward with your candidacy for this role."

And \*poof\*... just like that. My hopes evaporated like a fart in a hurricane.

Each email chipped away a piece of me...

I felt my identity as a Senior Engineer, with close to 6 years under my belt in DevOps, SRE, and Platform Engineering roles, unraveling. Imposter syndrome had never hit harder... I felt like a fraud.

I told myself, after the 3rd rejection, that maybe I was just unlucky this time around, especially due to recent economic troubles (even though these companies were setting [Wall Street records](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/26/tech-layoffs-jump-in-january-as-alphabet-meta-microsoft-reach-high.html)). After the 5th, I blamed AI. After the 7th, I ran out of excuses.

How was I able to make it so far in so many notoriously difficult interview processes and still not land a ***single one***?. Why couldn't I seal the deal?

## Revelations

After pacing around my bedroom/office for hours, on and off, over the course of a week, with my thinking cap on, I became more aware as to the source of my being continually rejected. It was actually the topic of another excuse I ruminated over during one of those pacing sessions that lead the way, and that topic was **competition**.

### The Competition

> "Toto, I have a feeling we're not in 2020 anymore"
>
> - Tech Guy in Layoffland

2020\... Remembered as the year the ***Thing-That-Made-Everyone-Wear-Masks*** began, but it was also a year when companies were hiring tech workers faster than the Javascript community was pumping out web frameworks. A time when my LinkedIn and email inboxes were being inundated with recruiter spam. Aaahh back in good 'ol 2020, before the phrase **"hiring freeze"** was invented. If there was any time I could have nabbed a prestigious FAANG job, it would have been around the 2020-2021 timeline.

Unfortunately, it's 2024 and those times and opportunities are long gone. AI has come with the morbid promise to <INSERT_SOUTH_PARK_MEME> "tekur jrrbs". The economy has been a factor, maybe not for big tech, but definitely for other industries and the start-up scene. These factors, along with several others I won't go into, have contributed to what has been coined on Reddit, [The Great Layoff](https://www.reddit.com/r/Layoffs/comments/1dh7dix/great_resignation_now_great_layoff/).

Due to tech giants like Google, Facebook, Microsoft, and many other companies laying off [over a hundred thousand workers](https://layoffs.fyi/) to date, the flood gates have been opened. Hell, the ***whole dam*** has collapsed, and the market is overflowing with talent.

It's like The Hunger Games out here but with nerds, keyboards, and AI generated resumes, mercilessly clicking down hundreds of **Easy Apply** buttons on LinkedIn. To make matters worse, these aren't just your average nerds. These ones carry the sacred and highly esteemed LinkedIn bio description of ***"ex-<INSERT_FAANG_COMPANY"***.

What makes

SIDE NOTE: I know not ***all*** FAANG engineers are super talented and, equally, not ***all*** super talented engineers are FAANGers. Just using the term as a catchall for the convenience of writing.

### What The Competition Revealed

As I've mentioned before, I'd made it to the final rounds of interviews for some of the hottest tech companies out there with very difficult interview processes. I may not be the smartest cookie, but there was at least **something** that kept me from getting cut early. Why didn't my skills and experience get me over the finish line? I'm just as talented and as much an engineer as any FAANGer right?

Turns out... not really.

This may be a "hot take" but, for the most part, unless you've worked for a FAANG-like company, where the ludicrous scale of the problems (of which the great majority of companies don't even come close to experiencing) require ***actual engineering*** to design, develop, and maintain solutions to manage, then your (my) "engineer" position is just a rebrand of systems administrator. (I've got a post coming further addressing this and my gripe with the bastardized interpretation and implementation of DevOps in more detail).

Most of my career has been spent using, glueing together, or configuring tools and services built by ***actual engineers***. I'm, basically, just a digital plumber. Python, yaml, and Terraform - my glue; Linux, Jenkins, "The Cloud", and Kubernetes - the pipes; and the moneymaking software products - the waterworks fixtures (fountains) and appliances (drinking fountain) being piped together. Albeit, I've planned and delivered my fair share of "plumbing" projects, ranging from small and simple to reasonably large and complex, of which I'm proud of, since they served to bring value to the places I worked and prove my worth as a plumber, but plumbing, up to a certain scale, is not engineering.

I wish I could say my experience is uncommon within the DevOps space but, in fact, it's quite the opposite.

The limited skills I'd gained from such work, plus the experienceless knowledge I'd acquired from interview prep were, ultimately, deemed insufficient to persuade FAANG level companies to take a chance on me.

### Who's To Blame?

Despite the problems with DevOps and it's implementations, the fault, at the end of the day, lies with yours truly.

I grew too comfortable with just using tools and common architectures and designs I could easily Google and drop into any project without much thought. I rarely dove deeply into these things to really understand the engineering principles and decisions that went into their conception and when I did, the "deep dives" were just wasted hours in rabbit-holes that did not lead any further analysis or practice in order to gain meaningful insights or experience.

There's a lot of things I ***thought*** I knew, but the failed interviews and analysis of the competition exposed that a good chunk of my knowledge was mostly superficial and lacking experience.

## A New Path Forward

The fault doesn't lie with DevOps nor the companies who incorrectly implement it.
